narrative: The 1940s marked a significant moment in Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture. While there is limited documentation from this era, it is clear that protective styles were essential for Afro-textured hair during this time. Cornrows, a traditional hairstyle of African braiding practice, were likely worn by many women as they are still a staple in the African diaspora today. Bantu knots, which require kinky hair to form, may have also been popular among women with this hair texture. The Jheri curl, invented later but gaining popularity in subsequent decades, was not yet a mainstream style during the 1940s. Nonetheless, it is evident that Black and African women were embracing their natural textures and finding creative ways to protect and style their hair amidst the societal norms of the time. Unfortunately, due to limited documentation from this era, we can only speculate on the specific hairstyles and cultural practices that defined Black and African women's hair culture during the 1940s.
